assets.prompt: Use case: stylized-concept. Asset type: Design 2 collector playing-card BACK prototype, one flat full-card production illustration, exact 5:7 portrait composition. Primary request: an extraordinarily refined Chinese imperial porcelain-inspired card back, plausibly reflecting the taste of an eighteenth-century emperor collecting Ming and Tang art. Make this a serious decorative-arts design with the delicacy of museum-grade Jingdezhen porcelain painting. The primary visual language is Ming underglaze cobalt lotus scroll decoration: fine tapered brush outlines, rhythmically curling stems, exquisitely articulated lotus petals and pointed leaves, subtle varied cobalt washes and restrained pigment pooling, reserved luminous porcelain ivory negative space. Secondary influence: restrained Tang floral roundel and palmette rhythms, completely integrated into the Chinese floral grammar. Composition: narrow carefully ruled cobalt double-line perimeter, elegant repeating lotus border, central elongated oval floral reserve linked to an intricate but airy continuous scroll field. Balanced two-way playing-card back, every large motif has a rotated counterpart; no readable top, centered small eight-petal lotus roundel. The design must feel painstakingly painted by a master court porcelain painter, with organic calligraphic line sensitivity and impeccable ornamental proportion. Palette: only deep cobalt, varied soft washed blues and warm porcelain white. Flat ornament suitable for printing on paper; no shiny 3D ceramic rendering, no object photograph, no perspective, no shadow, no distressed surface, no faux gold gradients. Do not depict an emperor, dragon mascot, cartoon creature, face, text, lettering, seal, signature or pseudo-Chinese characters. No Art Nouveau, Persian arabesques, Western acanthus, generic modern luxury logo, clipart, thick comic outlines, digital vector simplification, or fantasy-game styling. Output one single back artwork, full composition visible with a slim white outer margin and softly rounded corners. This is an original design informed by historical decorative arts, not a copy of an existing card.

Use case: precise-object-edit. Image 1 is the edit target: a cobalt-blue playing-card back prototype. Image 2 is a HISTORICAL STYLE REFERENCE ONLY, a Chinese Ming Yongle lotus meiping from the National Palace Museum, Taipei. Correct the ornament in Image 1 to genuinely follow the Chinese porcelain brush grammar visible in Image 2. Retain a flat full-card 5:7 composition, cobalt blue on luminous ivory white, ruled border, floral overall subject, and balanced two-way decorative structure. Replace the overly broad Western acanthus-looking leaves and European urn-shaped central reserve with slender sinuous CHINESE lotus stems, small pointed turned leaves, sharply lobed lotus leaves, articulated lotus blossoms seen in profile, and graceful open spiral stems as painted on the historical vase. Use the vase's finely outlined small leaves, thin jointed twisting branches, and many separated islands of cobalt with generous breathing space. Lotus petals should have fine linear divisions and Ming-style blue wash pooling rather than airbrushed white glow. Reduce the floral motif scale and increase the finesse and complexity of the linework, as if painted with a superbly controlled very fine brush on imperial porcelain. Replace the large central oval reserve with a small circular Chinese floral roundel no more than one-quarter of the card width, surrounded by continuously weaving spacious lotus branches. Pair motifs under a half-turn so the back is visually reversible. Use narrow ornamental border zones inspired by the vase shoulder and foot, with repeated small Chinese floral scrolls separated by thin blue rules. Do not depict the vase or copy its silhouette; translate its authentic decoration into an original paper card design. No vase photograph, background scene, text, invented Chinese characters, dragons, human figures, gold, pseudo-Persian medallion, Western acanthus leaves, 3D bevels, cartoon outlines, modern vector simplification or thick blank lower margin. The flat card should fully occupy the output with a clean even slim porcelain-white margin and rounded corners. Aim for the rarefied taste of an eighteenth-century Chinese imperial collection of earlier Ming masterpieces. One back only.
